opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was one of the most energizing environments I've been in. What struck me first was how open everyone was. You had senior professors, postdocs, PhD students, and people from industry all sitting at the same tables, and nobody really cared about titles. If you had an idea, people would just turn to you and say, "Okay, walk me through it," and suddenly you're at a whiteboard for an hour.

There was also a real sense of urgency. Things in AI, especially around large models and systems, were moving so fast that people felt they were working on problems that would matter immediately, not in ten years. So the conversations went beyond the theoretical. People were asking what we could build, what was actually bottlenecking us, and whether the infrastructure could keep up with the models.

At the same time, it had that very academic, Princeton quality, quiet and reflective. Between sessions, people would walk around campus and keep debating. Some of my most useful conversations happened over coffee or on those walks rather than in the formal talks.

For me personally, it was a reminder of why I love research. You're surrounded by people who are deeply curious and generous with their thinking, and you leave with more questions than you came in with, in a good way. A few collaborations and ideas I worked on later trace back to conversations from that week.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The workshop at Princeton was honestly one of the more energizing gatherings I've been to in a while. It was relatively small, so it felt less like a conference and more like a long conversation among people who all cared about the same problems.

What struck me most was how open everyone was. People weren't just presenting polished results. They were sharing half-finished ideas, things that didn't work, questions they hadn't figured out yet. That kind of honesty is rare at bigger venues, where there's pressure to look like you have everything figured out.

There was also a nice mix of people. You had folks from systems, from machine learning, from theory, and the hallway conversations often ended up being more valuable than the talks themselves. I remember several discussions that started over coffee and ran straight through lunch, just because someone asked a question nobody could answer cleanly.

And the setting helped. Princeton has that quiet campus feel, so you could actually step away, walk around, and think. I came back with a notebook full of ideas and a few new collaborators, which is really the best outcome you can hope for from something like that.
